pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 5-7 (KS1/Grades K-2): the butterfly life cycle — egg → caterpillar (larva) → chrysalis (pupa) → butterfly — and the big idea that these are STAGES OF ONE CREATURE, not four different animals.
• Standards — UK (DfE): KS1 Y2 'Living things and their habitats' contexts and animal life-cycle content; Y2 'Animals, including humans' (notice that animals have offspring which grow into adults — life cycles). Working-scientifically: observing changes over time.
• Standards — US (NGSS): 3-LS1-1 ([curriculum wording omitted; reference 3-LS1-1] birth, growth, reproduction and death) — the KS1 version is the observational precursor.
• Operational details — the transformation is the wonder AND the tricky bit: children must grasp that the caterpillar and butterfly are the SAME individual. Best taught by observing a real class caterpillar culture over weeks (first-hand change over time). Emphasise ordered SEQUENCE and that it is a cycle (the butterfly lays eggs again). Names: larva/pupa can be introduced alongside caterpillar/chrysalis.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 5): names the four stages. Tier B (age 6): puts the four stages in the correct order. Tier C (age 7): explains that it is one creature changing (metamorphosis) and that the cycle repeats.
bestPractices: Observe a real class caterpillar culture over weeks so children witness the change over time first-hand — the single most effective approach.
Hammer the 'same creature' idea — track one individual through all four stages so children don't think they are four different animals.
Teach it as an ordered CYCLE that repeats (butterfly lays eggs), not a one-way line.
Introduce the technical names (larva, pupa) alongside the familiar ones (caterpillar, chrysalis) without overloading.
Use time-based media (slider, timelapse) so the slow transformation is visible in one sitting.
keyRepresentations: A circular four-stage life-cycle diagram (egg → caterpillar → chrysalis → butterfly → egg).
A timelapse/scrubbable animation of the transformation.
A single highlighted individual carried through every stage.
commonMisconceptions: 'The caterpillar and butterfly are different animals' — the central misconception; they are one creature at different stages.
'The stages can happen in any order' — the sequence is fixed.
'The chrysalis is asleep/an egg' — not understanding it is the transforming pupa stage.
'It's a straight line that ends at butterfly' — missing that the cycle repeats.
'All baby animals look like small adults' — overgeneralising; metamorphosis is different from simple growth.

learn.summary: For ages 5–7, teach the butterfly life cycle (egg → caterpillar/larva → chrysalis/pupa → butterfly) as the STAGES OF ONE CREATURE changing, not four different animals. Centre the work on (1) ordering the four stages as a repeating cycle and (2) grasping that the caterpillar and butterfly are the same individual transforming, with the chrysalis as where the body is rebuilt. First-hand observation of a real class caterpillar culture over weeks anchors change-over-time; sequence/animation and labelled-diagram activities reinforce order, vocabulary and the same-creature idea.

activities.title: Observe a real class caterpillar culture over weeks
feedback: If a learner says the caterpillar died and a new butterfly appeared, revisit the day-by-day photos of the one named individual and trace the connecting arrows as a single continuous story.
If a learner says the stages could happen in any order, lay their own dated pictures in time order to show the sequence is fixed.
activities.rationale: First-hand observation of change over time lets children witness the transformation of one creature directly, which supports the central 'same creature' idea and the ordered sequence. Following a single named individual guards against the 'four different animals' misconception.
sourceClaims: First-hand observation of a class caterpillar culture over weeks is the recommended way to teach the butterfly life cycle and the same-creature idea.
KS1 pupils learn that animals have offspring which grow into adults (life cycles) and observe changes over time; the butterfly life cycle is a standard KS1 context.
learnerActions: Keep a class caterpillar culture and look at it regularly over several weeks.
Track and name ONE individual caterpillar, recording what it looks like each day with a drawing or photo.
Draw arrows connecting your day-by-day pictures to show it is one creature's story moving through caterpillar → chrysalis → butterfly (starting from the egg only if your culture began with eggs).
After the butterfly emerges, say aloud whether it is the same creature you have been watching and how you know.
activities.intendedInsight: The caterpillar and the butterfly are the SAME individual changing over time; the stages happen in a fixed order and take real time.

activities.title: Order the four stages into a repeating ring
feedback: If cards are placed in the wrong order, point to which stage comes before and after and ask what the creature would need to do to get there.
If a learner lays the cards in a straight line, ask 'what does the butterfly do next?' to reveal that eggs restart the cycle.
activities.rationale: Physically sequencing and forming a closed ring makes the ordered, cyclical structure concrete and addresses both the 'any order' and 'straight line that ends' misconceptions. Optional: a scrubbable time-slider or timelapse animation can let children watch the caterpillar grow, hang up and shed its skin to form a chrysalis, and emerge as a butterfly, with a highlight following the one individual — an example interaction, not a required mechanism.
sourceClaims: KS1 pupils learn that animals have offspring which grow into adults (life cycles) and observe changes over time; the butterfly life cycle is a standard KS1 context.
learnerActions: Take four shuffled picture cards — a tiny egg, a fat caterpillar, a chrysalis, a butterfly.
Arrange them into a RING rather than a straight line, so the cycle can start again.
Place a card showing the butterfly laying eggs on a leaf to close the loop back to the egg.
Say out loud why it is a cycle that repeats and not a line that ends at the butterfly.
activities.intendedInsight: The life cycle has a fixed order AND it repeats — the butterfly lays eggs that hatch into new caterpillars, so the cycle begins again with the next generation (the butterfly itself does not turn back into an egg).

activities.title: Label the cycle and learn both names for each stage
feedback: If a learner describes the chrysalis as 'sleeping', contrast sleeping (wake up the same) with transforming (come out a different shape) using before/after images.
If a learner introduces only one name, prompt for its partner term (caterpillar↔larva, chrysalis↔pupa).
activities.rationale: A tap-to-reveal labelled diagram can teach vocabulary and order and introduce technical names alongside familiar ones without overload. A labelled diagram presents order and names clearly but does not itself show the transformation; pair it with observation or animation so the change is also seen.
learnerActions: Work with a circular four-stage diagram and reveal a short fact about each stage (egg, caterpillar, chrysalis, butterfly).
For each stage, match the familiar name to the technical name: caterpillar = larva, chrysalis = pupa.
Say what is happening at each stage, including that inside the chrysalis the caterpillar's body is being rebuilt (not sleeping).
activities.intendedInsight: Each stage has a name and a role; the technical terms larva and pupa name the caterpillar and chrysalis stages, and the chrysalis is where the body transforms.

activities.title: Retell or draw the transformation
feedback: If a retelling skips the chrysalis or treats it as a pause, ask what is happening to the body inside while we cannot see.

If the drawing shows the caterpillar simply 'growing wings', compare caterpillar and butterfly body parts (legs, mouth, wings) and ask 'where did the extra legs go?' to show a full rebuild, not an add-on.
activities.rationale: Producing a retelling or drawing requires the child to construct the sequence and the same-creature explanation, going beyond recognition. Comparing body parts targets the 'just grows wings' misconception. This production benefit is a research-informed proposal; no provided source directly establishes it.
learnerActions: After reading a story (e.g. The Very Hungry Caterpillar, which calls the chrysalis a 'cocoon' — real butterflies form a chrysalis, while moths spin cocoons) or watching the real change happen, retell the transformation from caterpillar to butterfly.
Draw the sequence, showing the same creature at each stage.
Answer: is the butterfly the same creature that was the caterpillar, or a new one, and how do you know?
activities.intendedInsight: Children can reconstruct the ordered transformation themselves and explain it as one creature changing.

activities.title: Compare different kinds of change (extension)
feedback: If a learner says all baby animals look like small adults, contrast the caterpillar→butterfly rebuild with the grasshopper nymph, which already looks much like a small adult and mostly gets bigger as its wings grow.
Credit answers that reason about whether the body shape is rebuilt, not just whether the animal gets larger.
activities.rationale: Transfer to counterexamples (grasshopper incomplete metamorphosis; frog) reveals whether the child understands transformation rather than a memorised list, and addresses the overgeneralisation that all young look like small adults.
sourceClaims: Students learn that organisms have diverse life cycles but all include birth, growth, reproduction and death (3-LS1-1); KS1 work is the observational precursor.
learnerActions: Consider a grasshopper, which hatches as a nymph that looks like a small grasshopper without working wings, and grows bigger by shedding its skin several times, with its wings developing gradually and no chrysalis.
Consider a tadpole that turns into a frog.
For each, say whether the change is more like the caterpillar's story (a big body rebuild) or more like simple growing bigger, and why.
activities.intendedInsight: A dramatic whole-body change (like caterpillar to butterfly, or tadpole to frog) is different from mostly growing bigger, where the young already looks much like a small adult (like a grasshopper nymph, which has no chrysalis); this distinguishes real understanding from memorised stages.

constraints: Core objective: children must grasp that the caterpillar and butterfly are the SAME individual at different stages, and that the sequence is a repeating cycle — not just name or order the four stages.

First-hand observation over weeks is time-dependent; a scrubbable animation or timelapse is a useful complement that compresses the slow change into one sitting but is not a substitute for watching a real change over time where feasible.

Picture-card ordering and labelled diagrams are scaffolds for order and vocabulary; on their own they do not show the transformation. Pair them with observation or animation so the same-creature change is actually witnessed.

Recognition/matching and multiple-choice tasks assess order, names and the same-creature idea but do not by themselves elicit independent retelling or explanation; include at least one production task (retell or draw).
Introduce technical names (larva, pupa) alongside familiar ones (caterpillar, chrysalis) without overloading young learners.

Diagnosis lives in the 'why', not the yes/no: a child may order the stages correctly yet still believe the caterpillar dies and a new butterfly is born. Always probe the reasoning behind the chrysalis stage.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Source claims are marked verified:false in the row; cited standards (DfE KS1; NGSS 3-LS1-1) and the 'class culture is the recommended way' practice claim were not independently re-checked here.

The original artefact notes asserted that animation is 'the emotional core' and that 3D/conversation formats are less direct; these are catalog-fit opinions, not established comparative efficacy. They have been softened to optional affordances rather than claims that one medium is necessary or that others teach less.

The source's own correctAnswer describes the chrysalis as the body being 'rebuilt/reorganised'; this is biologically reasonable for this age but simplified. Kept at an age-appropriate level ('the body is rebuilt') without overclaiming cellular detail.

The grasshopper nymph and frog comparisons come from the assessment probes and are retained as an extension; they are age-appropriate counterexamples but the teacher should keep the framing simple (rebuild vs. just getting bigger).
Activity 3 (labelling and technical names) carries sourceClaims:[] because no provided source directly supports the vocabulary-teaching principle; it remains an unvalidated proposal.

Activity 4 (retell or draw) now carries sourceClaims:[]: claim 1 supports the life-cycle topic and observation but not the production-task principle (retelling/drawing beyond recognition), which remains an unvalidated proposal.

Activity 2 (order into a ring) retains claim 1 because it explicitly references 'life cycles' (the cyclical content), but this is content/topic-level support only and is not evidence that the card-ordering interaction is effective.

probeDeeper: 'When the butterfly comes out, is it the SAME creature that was the caterpillar, or a new one? How do you know?'

'A grasshopper hatches as a tiny grasshopper (a nymph) and just gets bigger — no chrysalis. Is that the same as the caterpillar's story, or different?' (a real counterexample: incomplete metamorphosis)
'What is actually happening inside the chrysalis while we can't see?'
'A tadpole turns into a frog. Is that more like the caterpillar's change, or like the grasshopper's?'
assess.correctAnswer: It is not right — the caterpillar does NOT die. It is the SAME animal changing its body. Inside the chrysalis the caterpillar's body is rebuilt (reorganised) into a butterfly. So one creature goes through stages: egg → caterpillar → chrysalis → butterfly. It transforms; it is not replaced by a new animal.

errorPatterns.pattern: Believes the caterpillar and butterfly are two separate animals — 'the caterpillar dies and the butterfly is a different creature'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Follow one named caterpillar through photos day by day into and out of the chrysalis. Emphasise it is the SAME individual the whole time — draw arrows connecting the stages as one creature's story, not four animals.
errorPatterns.distractor: They are two different animals — the caterpillar dies and a new butterfly is born
errorPatterns.revealedBy: States the caterpillar dies / disappears and a new butterfly is born; treats them as unrelated animals rather than one life cycle

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks the caterpillar is just asleep/resting in the chrysalis and wakes up as a butterfly, with no real change of body
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show that inside the chrysalis the body is reorganised — the caterpillar's legs, wings and shape all change. Contrast 'sleeping' (wakes up the same) with 'transforming' (comes out a different shape) using before/after images.
errorPatterns.distractor: The caterpillar is just sleeping in the chrysalis and wakes up as a butterfly
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Second tier: describes the chrysalis as sleeping or hiding, not as the body being rebuilt

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks the caterpillar simply 'grows wings' and stays basically the same body — misses that the whole body reorganises
errorPatterns.nextMove: Compare caterpillar and butterfly body parts directly (number of legs, mouth, wings). Ask 'where did the extra legs go?' to show it is a full rebuild, not an add-on.
errorPatterns.distractor: The caterpillar just grows wings and turns into a butterfly
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the caterpillar sprouts wings and keeps crawling; no sense of a rebuilt body or a chrysalis stage

responseLevels.gap: Says the caterpillar and butterfly are different animals, or that the caterpillar dies / is just sleeping; no idea of one continuous creature.
responseLevels.full: States it is the same creature transforming, explains the chrysalis as where the body is reorganised, AND transfers the idea — e.g. recognises the grasshopper nymph or frog as a different or similar kind of change, showing an understanding of transformation rather than memorised stages.
responseLevels.partial: Can list the stages (egg, caterpillar, chrysalis, butterfly) in order but describes them as separate events — cannot say it is ONE creature whose body is rebuilt in the chrysalis, or slips back to 'a new butterfly comes out'.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A child says: 'The caterpillar and the butterfly are two different animals — the caterpillar dies inside the chrysalis and a brand-new butterfly comes out.' Is that right? Tell me what really happens, and why.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands metamorphosis says the caterpillar and butterfly are ONE creature and the chrysalis is where the body is rebuilt. A child holding the common 'separate creatures' idea insists the caterpillar died and the butterfly is new — and the second-tier 'why?' exposes it, because they explain the chrysalis as a death/birth or as 'just sleeping' rather than as transformation of one continuous body. The reason, not the yes/no, is where the misconception lives.
